title: Direct/adaptive-mixture phase-gradient learning for neural-network quantum states with complex phase structure
authors: Yi-Ran Xue, Rui Wang, Baigeng Wang, Chenan Wei
abstract: Neural-network quantum states (NQS) are a leading variational tool for quantum many-body physics, yet their optimization is fragile whenever the ground state carries a non-trivial sign or complex phase structure, a situation generic to gauge fields, broken time-reversal symmetry, and fermionic statistics. We trace this fragility to the stochastic estimator of the phase gradient rather than to network expressiveness. The phase sector of the Monte Carlo energy gradient is a noisy score-function estimator; differentiating the local energy instead yields a direct estimator that is unbiased for the same phase force, has far lower variance, and requires only a separated amplitude--phase ansatz. Demonstrated on a 100-site flux ladder, a small network trained this way reaches $0.89\%$ median error, where tuned standard baselines plateau at $1.8\%$ and wider or deeper standard-gradient networks degrade from $8.4\%$ to $24.6\%$. The advantage carries over to chiral XXX chains: the direct estimator again converges to a markedly lower error than the standard one, across $α$ and size; it grows with flux and vanishes in zero-flux controls. An adaptive-mixture of the two estimators is provably never worse in variance than the better endpoint at the optimal mixing coefficient, with seed-resolved diagnostics tracing much of the gain to eliminating failed runs. Estimator design thus emerges as a first-class lever for complex-valued neural quantum states.
summary: This paper addresses the critical issue of noisy phase gradient estimation when using Neural Network Quantum States (NQS) for complex quantum many-body systems. The authors introduce a theoretically superior direct estimator and an adaptive mixture that combines it with standard methods. This combination dramatically reduces optimization variance, enabling accurate simulations in regimes characterized by complex phases, such as those found in synthetic gauge fields.
main_problem: The optimization of Neural-Network Quantum States (NQS) is fragile when the ground state possesses a non-trivial complex phase structure, leading to convergence stalls.
main_result: A direct local energy derivative estimator ($\hat{g}_{dir}$) and an adaptive mixture combining it with the standard score-function estimator significantly reduce variance, achieving much lower errors than standard methods on flux ladder systems.
method: The authors compare three estimators for the phase gradient force: a standard stochastic estimator, a direct local energy derivative estimator, and a theoretically derived adaptive mixture of the two. The advantage is shown to stem from noise reduction in the estimator itself.
model_or_system: The work uses NQS parameterized by separated amplitude-phase ansatzes to simulate quantum many-body systems, benchmarked on a 100-site flux ladder (gauge fields) and chiral XXX chains.
key_observables: Median relative error of the phase gradient force convergence; variance ($	ext{Var}$) and covariance ($	ext{Cov}$) between estimators.
important_parameters: Flux strength ($\Phi$), system size ($L=100$ sites), mixing coefficient ($\lambda$).
main_assumptions: The method assumes a separated amplitude-phase parameterization for the direct estimator; convergence analysis relies on idealized flow bounds and is not claimed for all arbitrary network structures.
figures_summary: Figures compare training trajectories showing that $\hat{g}_{dir}$ significantly outperforms standard baselines, especially when networks are widened or deepened. The adaptive mixture trajectory ($\lambda$) shows a dynamic shift towards the low-variance direct signal during optimization.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem (phase gradient noise), introduces and analyzes two estimators ($\hat{g}_{std}$ vs $\hat{g}_{dir}$), develops the theoretically optimal adaptive mixture, and validates its superior performance across multiple complex physical benchmarks.
why_interesting: For a theoretical physicist working on AMO or open quantum systems, this work provides a crucial computational tool for simulating Hamiltonians with inherent gauge fields or non-trivial topology, allowing access to regimes previously limited by numerical noise.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Training dynamics on the 100-site flux ladder. All panels use the L = 50 flux ladder (100 sites, half filling), an MLP with width 128 and depth 2, batch size 1024, 48 MCMC sweeps per optimization step, and base learning rate η = 0.03. (a) Energy training curves at Φ = 0.2π, with DMRG reference Eref = −44.826. (b) Relative-error training curves at Φ = 0.2π. (c) Energy training curves at Φ = 0.3π, with DMRG reference Eref = −43.303. (d) Relative-error training curves at Φ = 0.3π. Solid lines show means, dotted lines medians, and shaded bands interquartile ranges.

Fig. 2 Tail-window performance on the 100-site flux ladder. All panels use the same runs and convergence-window convention as Fig. 1. (a) Tail-window relative-error statistics at Φ = 0.2π. (b) Tail-window energies at Φ = 0.2π. (c) Tail-window relative-error statistics at Φ = 0.3π. (d) Tail-window energies at Φ = 0.3π. Bars show means, horizontal lines medians, whiskers interquartile ranges, and points individual numeric seeds.

Fig. 3 The estimator advantage is not removed by wider or deeper standard-gradient networks. The benchmark is the L = 50 (100-site) flux ladder at Φ = 0.3π, trained for 50,000 steps with the same optimizer settings as Fig. 1. (a) Width sweep comparing direct and standard phase- gradient training at fixed depth 2 for MLP widths 128 and 256. (b) Shallow direct phase-gradient performance for width 128, depth 2 compared with standard-gradient MLPs of width 128, depth 2; width 256, depth 2; and width 128, depth 4. The shallow direct phase-gradient network reaches a median tail-window error below 1%, while standard phase-gradient networks remain substantially worse after increasing width or depth.

Fig. 4 Representative ResNet comparison at Φ = 0.3π. The system is again the L = 50 (100-site) flux ladder; the MLP is replaced by a ResNet ansatz and trained for 40,000 optimization steps. (a) Energy convergence for direct and standard phase-gradient training. (b) Relative-error convergence for the same runs. The direct phase-gradient estimator continues descending towards the DMRG reference, whereas the standard phase-gradient run plateaus well above it.
